claim: Response variability arises from fluctuations in the internal state of the brain, which modulate how sensory information is represented and transformed to guide behavioral actions.
source: Response variability is an essential and universal feature of sensory processing and behavior. It arises from fluctuations in the internal state of the brain, which modulate how sensory information is represented and transformed to guide behavioral actions.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study, but draws on established scientific understanding.

claim: Brain state is shaped by recent network activity, fed back through recurrent connections to modulate neuronal excitability.
source: In part, brain state is shaped by recent network activity, fed back through recurrent connections to modulate neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: A minimal network model incorporating fast, short range, recurrent excitation and long-lasting, activity-dependent suppression reproduced intermittent bursting in the optic tectum.
source: We developed a minimal network model incorporating fast, short range, recurrent excitation and long-lasting, activity-dependent suppression that reproduced a hallmark property of tectal activity – intermittent bursting.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Model-estimated excitability state based on recent activity history explained a portion of trial-to-trial variability in visually evoked responses.
source: We next used the model to estimate the excitability state of tectal neurons based on recent activity history and found that this explained a portion of the trial-to-trial variability in visually evoked responses, as well as spatially selective response adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 4.

claim: Model dynamics predicted behavioral trends such as selective habituation of visually evoked prey-catching.
source: Moreover, these dynamics also predicted behavioral trends such as selective habituation of visually evoked prey-catching.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Repeated presentation of identical sensory cues typically evokes variable activity.
source: Consequently, repeated presentation of identical sensory cues typically evokes variable activity and this variation is left unexplained by analyses restricted to response averaging, as is traditionally used for empirically estimating neuronal tuning properties.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation in neuroscience.

claim: Internal state is influenced by activity of neuromodulatory populations.
source: Internal state is multidimensional and influenced by many factors including activity of neuromodulatory populations (Nicola et al., 2003; Marques et al., 2019; Mu et al., 2019; McCormick et al., 2020) and short- and long-term changes in synaptic strength (Magee and Grienberger, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Internal state is influenced by short- and long-term changes in synaptic strength.
source: Internal state is multidimensional and influenced by many factors including activity of neuromodulatory populations (Nicola et al., 2003; Marques et al., 2019; Mu et al., 2019; McCormick et al., 2020) and short- and long-term changes in synaptic strength (Magee and Grienberger, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Recent network activity influences single neuron excitability through local and/or long-range recurrent connections.
source: One factor that influences single neuron excitability is recent network activity, fed back by local and/or long-range recurrent connections (Mohajerani et al., 2013; Zylbertal et al., 2017a; Smith et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activity may briefly shift the excitability of post-synaptic neurons as a result of direct synaptic transmission.
source: For example, activity may briefly shift the excitability of post-synaptic neurons as a result of direct synaptic transmission, or exert longer-term changes through secondary processes such as vesicle release dynamics (Shu et al., 2006) or modulation of intrinsic properties (e.g. ion channel dynamics; Zhang and Sillar, 2012; Zylbertal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is presented as an example mechanism with supporting citations.

claim: Activity may exert longer-term changes in excitability through vesicle release dynamics.
source: For example, activity may briefly shift the excitability of post-synaptic neurons as a result of direct synaptic transmission, or exert longer-term changes through secondary processes such as vesicle release dynamics (Shu et al., 2006) or modulation of intrinsic properties (e.g. ion channel dynamics; Zhang and Sillar, 2012; Zylbertal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Activity may exert longer-term changes in excitability through modulation of intrinsic properties such as ion channel dynamics.
source: For example, activity may briefly shift the excitability of post-synaptic neurons as a result of direct synaptic transmission, or exert longer-term changes through secondary processes such as vesicle release dynamics (Shu et al., 2006) or modulation of intrinsic properties (e.g. ion channel dynamics; Zhang and Sillar, 2012; Zylbertal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ongoing activity is commonplace in sensorimotor brain regions, including multiple cortical areas and the optic tectum.
source: Such activity is commonplace in sensorimotor brain regions, including multiple cortical areas (Kenet et al., 2003; Yuste et al., 2005), and the optic tectum (OT; Romano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ongoing activity is a cause of fluctuations in network state, as evidenced by the variability it introduces to sensory responses.
source: Ongoing activity is, on the one hand, a cause of fluctuations in network state, as evidenced by the variability it introduces to sensory responses (Arieli et al., 1996; Petersen et al., 2003; He, 2013; Shimaoka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Patterns of ongoing activity are a consequence of brain state dynamics and may be altered for extended periods of time by transient inputs.
source: Conversely, patterns of ongoing activity are also a consequence of brain state dynamics and may be altered for extended periods of time by transient inputs (Fiser et al., 2004; Abbott et al., 2009; Deneux and Grinvald, 2016; Chen and Gong, 2019; Franco and Yaksi, 2021; Fritsche et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ongoing activity typically displays a characteristic correlation structure between individual neurons and across time.
source: This bidirectional nature, along with the observations that ongoing activity typically displays a characteristic correlation structure between individual neurons and across time (Tsodyks et al., 1999; Kenet et al., 2003; Smith and Kohn, 2008; Smith et al., 2018) and recapitulates some features of sensory-evoked activity (Luczak et al., 2009), makes it an attractive handle for studying the spatiotemporal relationships between neural activity and network state.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ongoing activity recapitulates some features of sensory-evoked activity.
source: This bidirectional nature, along with the observations that ongoing activity typically displays a characteristic correlation structure between individual neurons and across time (Tsodyks et al., 1999; Kenet et al., 2003; Smith and Kohn, 2008; Smith et al., 2018) and recapitulates some features of sensory-evoked activity (Luczak et al., 2009), makes it an attractive handle for studying the spatiotemporal relationships between neural activity and network state.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Light-sheet calcium imaging was performed on transgenic larvae expressing GCaMP6s at 6 dpf.
source: To measure this activity, we performed light-sheet calcium imaging of transgenic larvae expressing GCaMP6s (elavl3:H2B-GCaMP6s, 6 dpf, n=14), initially under constant environmental conditions (i.e. without presenting visual stimuli).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: A 375x410 × 75 μm volume encompassing OT and adjacent brain structures was imaged at a rate of 5 volumes per second.
source: We imaged a 375x410 × 75 μm volume encompassing OT and adjacent brain structures, at a rate of 5 volumes per second (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters used in the study, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: On average, 1.4×10^4±3×10^3 tectal SPV cells per fish were analyzed.
source: Imaged volumes were registered to a reference brain (Avants et al., 2009; Marquart et al., 2015) and somata in the stratum periventriculare (SPV), which comprise the majority of tectal neurons, were considered for further analysis (Figure 1B, 1.4‧104±3‧103 tectal SPV cells per fish, mean ± SD).
evidence: This reports the number of cells analyzed per fish, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Pairwise activity correlation decreased as a function of Euclidean distance between neurons.
source: Correlation coefficients smoothly and monotonically decreased as a function of the Euclidean distance between neurons (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis, shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: The spatial pattern of activity correlations was compatible with recurrent excitatory interactions between tectal cells.
source: The spatial pattern of activity correlations was compatible with recurrent excitatory interactions between tectal cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation data presented in Figure 1.

claim: A 2D Gaussian fitted to correlation maps yielded good fits for most cells (r2=0.42 ± 0.17, mean ± SD).
source: A 2D Gaussian was fitted to each map, excluding the seed neuron itself, yielding good fits for most cells (r2=0.42 ± 0.17, mean ± SD, Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This reports the quality of Gaussian fits to the correlation data.

claim: The peaks of fitted Gaussians showed close correspondence to the locations of seed neurons.
source: The peaks of the fitted Gaussians showed close correspondence to the locations of seed neurons (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Comparably good fits were obtained by fitting an exponential decay function (r2=0.39 ± 0.18, mean ± SD).
source: Comparably good fits were obtained by fitting an exponential decay function (r2=0.39 ± 0.18, mean ± SD), and again the peaks of fitted exponentials corresponded to the locations of seed neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This reports the quality of exponential fits to the correlation data.

claim: A salient aspect of tectal activity is the occurrence of 'spontaneous' bursts, during which spatially compact groups of neurons briefly fire in synchrony.
source: A salient aspect of tectal activity is the occurrence of 'spontaneous' bursts, during which spatially compact groups of neurons briefly fire in synchrony (Bianco and Engert, 2015; Romano et al., 2015; Avitan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an established observation with supporting citations.

claim: 54,424 bursts were identified in 14 fish.
source: Overall, 54,424 bursts were identified in 14 fish.
evidence: This reports the total number of bursts detected in the study.

claim: On average, each activity peak was associated with 1.5±2.0 localised bursts (mean ± SD).
source: On average, each activity peak was associated with 1.5±2.0 localised bursts (mean ± SD), bursts occurred at a rate of 46±11 per minute and appeared uniformly distributed in space and time (Figure 1G).
evidence: This reports statistics about burst occurrence from the data analysis.

claim: Bursts occurred at a rate of 46±11 per minute.
source: On average, each activity peak was associated with 1.5±2.0 localised bursts (mean ± SD), bursts occurred at a rate of 46±11 per minute and appeared uniformly distributed in space and time (Figure 1G).
evidence: This reports the rate of burst occurrence from the data.

claim: Bursts appeared uniformly distributed in space and time.
source: On average, each activity peak was associated with 1.5±2.0 localised bursts (mean ± SD), bursts occurred at a rate of 46±11 per minute and appeared uniformly distributed in space and time (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial and temporal distribution of bursts shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The majority of spiking during bursts occurred over a timecourse of around one second.
source: Bursts were brisk, phasic events, with the majority of spiking occurring over a timecourse of around one second (Figure 1H).
evidence: This describes the temporal profile of bursts shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The sizes and durations of bursts were highly variable (95±183 neurons per burst, 2.5±3 s duration, mean ± SD).
source: As has been previously reported, the sizes and durations of bursts were highly variable (95±183 neurons per burst, 2.5±3 s duration, mean ± SD), and distributed according to a power law (Figure 1I–J), suggestive of a critical phenomenon with 'avalanche' dynamics (Ponce-Alvarez et al., 2018).
evidence: This reports statistics about burst characteristics from the data analysis.

claim: Burst sizes and durations were distributed according to a power law.
source: As has been previously reported, the sizes and durations of bursts were highly variable (95±183 neurons per burst, 2.5±3 s duration, mean ± SD), and distributed according to a power law (Figure 1I–J), suggestive of a critical phenomenon with 'avalanche' dynamics (Ponce-Alvarez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1I-J, with interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Power law distribution of burst sizes and durations is suggestive of a critical phenomenon with 'avalanche' dynamics.
source: As has been previously reported, the sizes and durations of bursts were highly variable (95±183 neurons per burst, 2.5±3 s duration, mean ± SD), and distributed according to a power law (Figure 1I–J), suggestive of a critical phenomenon with 'avalanche' dynamics (Ponce-Alvarez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the power law distribution, supported by citation.

claim: Cells were less active for tens of seconds after participating in a burst.
source: Cells were less active and less likely to take part in another burst for tens of seconds.
evidence: This is an observation from the burst-triggered activity analysis shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Cells were less likely to take part in another burst for tens of seconds after participating in a burst.
source: Cells were less active and less likely to take part in another burst for tens of seconds.
evidence: This is an observation from the burst-triggered participation analysis shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Ongoing tectal activity is compatible with excitatory recurrent connectivity that smoothly decays with distance.
source: In sum, ongoing tectal activity is compatible with two types of intercellular interaction that might shape network dynamics. First, activity correlation is suggestive of excitatory recurrent connectivity that smoothly decays with distance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis presented in Figure 1C-E.

claim: The dynamics of bursting suggest prolonged activity-dependent suppression of excitability.
source: Second, the dynamics of bursting suggest prolonged activity-dependent suppression of excitability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the burst statistics and post-burst suppression shown in Figure 1I-L.

claim: Recurrent excitatory connectivity, balanced by long-range inhibition, produces stable, self-sustaining and spatially defined 'blobs' of activity.
source: Theoretical network analysis has proposed that recurrent excitatory connectivity, balanced by long-range inhibition, produces stable, self-sustaining and spatially defined 'blobs' of activity (Amari, 1977).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: Making inhibition depend on slow time-integration of activity would produce transient bursts instead of stable blobs.
source: We reasoned that by making the inhibition in such a model depend on a slow time-integration of activity, transient bursts would emerge instead of stable blobs and would be followed by prolonged activity suppression.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that motivated the model design.

claim: The LNP model framework has been successfully used to relate activity in neuronal populations to past activity and sensory input.
source: This framework has been successfully used to relate activity in neuronal populations to past activity and sensory input (Pillow et al., 2005; Pillow et al., 2008; Truccolo et al., 2005), and its non-deterministic aspect fits the apparent stochastic nature of tectal bursting.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using this framework.

claim: The network model is fully described by seven parameters and the locations of neurons.
source: Notably, given that the same connectivity rule is applied to every tectal cell, the network is fully described by the set of seven parameters and the locations of the neurons.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model design.

claim: Using the generative model to simulate network activity resulted in spatially localised bursting.
source: In accordance with our hypothesis, using this generative model to simulate network activity resulted in spatially localised bursting (Video 1).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulations, shown in Video 1.

claim: Bursting was a robust emergent property observed across a broad range of parameter values.
source: Bursting was a robust emergent property that was observed across a broad range of parameter values (see below).
evidence: This is an observation from parameter exploration of the model.

claim: Bursts in the simulation were uniformly distributed in space and time with a range of sizes and durations.
source: Bursts could be identified by analysing the simulation spiking output using the same method as for experimental data (described above) and were uniformly distributed in space and time with a range of sizes and durations (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is an observation from the model simulations shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: PCA-promax algorithm applied to simulated data yielded multiple spatially localised 'assemblies' despite no preferential connectivity.
source: We applied this method to our simulated tectal network and despite the fact that, by design, there were no subgroups of cells with preferential connectivity, PCA-promax yielded multiple spatially localised 'assemblies' (Figure 2D), as was also the case for recorded data (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a result from applying the PCA-promax algorithm to simulation data, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Repeated, synchronised bursting of tectal neurons can occur in a network where every cell has the same distance-based recurrent connectivity.
source: This analysis demonstrates that repeated, synchronised bursting of tectal neurons can occur in a network where every cell has the same distance-based recurrent connectivity and therefore that this feature of activity does not, by itself, imply the existence of preferentially connected subnetworks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PCA-promax analysis of the model.

claim: Bursts tend to occur in regions with higher than average excitability and leave behind a region of low excitability.
source: This revealed (Figure 2F, Video 2) that bursts tend to occur in regions with higher than average excitability (bright green) and leave behind a region of low excitability (black), supressing activity in the same region for a long period of time.
evidence: This is an observation from examining the linear drive in the model, shown in Figure 2F and Video 2.

claim: A simple recurrent interaction motif is sufficient to explain tectal bursting.
source: In sum, our network model reveals that a simple recurrent interaction motif is sufficient to explain tectal bursting.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Bursting occurred robustly across a range of parameter values, with burst statistics varying across parameter space.
source: We found that bursting occurred robustly across a range of parameter values, albeit with burst statistics – such as average burst size and duration – varying across parameter space.
evidence: This is an observation from systematic parameter exploration shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Bursting is robust to stochastic non-uniformities in connections from pruning random subsets of excitatory and inhibitory connections.
source: We also confirmed the capacity of the model to produce bursting with an exponential rather than Gaussian relationship between distance and connection strength (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and the robustness of the bursting phenomenon to stochastic non-uniformities in connections by pruning random subsets of excitatory and inhibitory connections (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is a result from model variants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bursting is a robust phenomenon but bursting statistics are modulated by the spatiotemporal parameters defining recurrent interactions.
source: These analyses indicate that bursting is a robust phenomenon but that bursting statistics are modulated by the spatiotemporal parameters defining recurrent interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the parameter exploration analyses.

claim: The optimized model successfully reproduced the bursting statistics of the zebrafish tectum.
source: The resulting optimized model was successful in reproducing the bursting statistics of the zebrafish tectum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, blue).
evidence: This is a result from the optimization procedure shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The optimized model reproduced features used as optimization objectives (burst sizes distribution, burst durations distribution, and post-burst activity suppression).
source: This was true for both the features used as optimization objectives (Figure 3B–D), as well as two that were not used for parameter tuning, namely burst-triggered burst participation probability (Figure 3E) and the burst temporal profile (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: The optimized model reproduced burst-triggered burst participation probability and burst temporal profile, which were not used for parameter tuning.
source: This was true for both the features used as optimization objectives (Figure 3B–D), as well as two that were not used for parameter tuning, namely burst-triggered burst participation probability (Figure 3E) and the burst temporal profile (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: A single spike in one neuron strongly excites its immediate neighbours for a brief moment (<1 s) while slightly reducing the excitability of a large part of the tectal hemisphere for tens of seconds.
source: As a result, a single spike in one neuron strongly excites its immediate neighbours for a brief moment (<1 s), while slightly reducing the excitability of a large part of the tectal hemisphere for tens of seconds (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is an observation from the optimized model shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Small moving spots evoke robust tectal activity.
source: We presented zebrafish with small moving spots, which evoke robust tectal activity (Figure 4A, Niell and Smith, 2005; Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The responses of tectal neurons displayed retinotopic mapping and direction selectivity.
source: The responses of tectal neurons displayed retinotopic mapping and direction selectivity (Figure 4B, Stuermer, 1988; Niell and Smith, 2005; Hunter et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 4B, supported by citations.

claim: Model-predicted excitability explained a substantial fraction of the trial-to-trial variability of visually evoked neural activity.
source: Model-predicted excitability explained a substantial fraction of the trial-to-trial variability of visually evoked neural activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: For individual neurons, a threshold-linear function described the visual responses across single trials in terms of the pre-stimulus linear drive.
source: Specifically, we found that for individual neurons, a threshold-linear function described the visual responses of the cell across single trials in terms of the pre-stimulus linear drive, estimated using the model, for those same trials (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Model-inferred linear drive explained response variability significantly better than a 'null' estimate using randomly sampled timepoints.
source: Model-inferred linear drive explained response variability significantly better than a 'null' estimate of network state, using randomly sampled timepoints, or states estimated using the baseline model parameters (Figure 4E, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E with statistical comparison.

claim: Model-inferred linear drive explained response variability significantly better than states estimated using the baseline model parameters.
source: Model-inferred linear drive explained response variability significantly better than a 'null' estimate of network state, using randomly sampled timepoints, or states estimated using the baseline model parameters (Figure 4E, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E with statistical comparison.

claim: Recent network activity in the vicinity of a neuron tends to suppress its excitability, resulting in a relatively reduced response to visual sensory input.
source: In sum, recent network activity in the vicinity of a neuron tends to supress its excitability, resulting in a relatively reduced response to visual sensory input.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of how pre-stimulus activity affects visual responses.

claim: Receptive fields collectively covered visual space, with an average width (2.5σ) of 38°±24° (mean ± SD).
source: Receptive fields collectively covered visual space, with an average width (2.5σ) of 38°±24° (mean ± SD, Figure 5B), comparable to previous reports (Niell and Smith, 2005).
evidence: This reports the receptive field properties from the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Neurons responsive to high and low elevation stimuli occupied distinct anatomical locations.
source: Because visual space is retinotopically mapped within OT, neurons responsive to high and low elevation stimuli occupied distinct anatomical locations (Figure 5C, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The model predicted a substantial, long-term reduction in tectal activity for tens of seconds following visual stimulation.
source: Running the network simulation with sensory input predicted a substantial, long-term reduction in tectal activity for tens of seconds following visual stimulation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model simulation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cells responsive to the recently presented stimulus were predicted to show a greater suppression of ongoing activity compared to neurons responsive to the other elevation.
source: Thus, cells responsive to the recently presented stimulus were predicted to show a greater suppression of ongoing activity in the period following stimulus offset as compared to neurons responsive to the other elevation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Spatial-selective suppression of activity was explained by a lasting state of low linear drive extending beyond the duration of the sensory stimulus.
source: This spatial-selective suppression of activity was explained by a lasting state of low linear drive extending beyond the duration of the sensory stimulus (Figure 5F, Video 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F and Video 3.

claim: Neurons responsive to the recently presented stimulus showed a marked reduction of ongoing activity for tens of seconds in experimental data.
source: As predicted by the model simulation, neurons responsive to the recently presented stimulus showed a marked reduction of ongoing activity for tens of seconds, whereas neurons responsive to the other elevation showed a lesser suppression of post-stimulus activity (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Neurons responsive to the other elevation showed a lesser suppression of post-stimulus activity.
source: As predicted by the model simulation, neurons responsive to the recently presented stimulus showed a marked reduction of ongoing activity for tens of seconds, whereas neurons responsive to the other elevation showed a lesser suppression of post-stimulus activity (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The network model can account for bidirectional interactions between neuronal activity and network state.
source: In sum, our network model can account for bidirectional interactions between neuronal activity and network state that lead to interactions between ongoing and stimulus-evoked tectal activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling and experimental results.

claim: Ongoing activity shapes the incidental state of neuronal excitability, which in turn modulates visual responses.
source: Ongoing activity shapes the incidental state of neuronal excitability, which in turn modulates visual responses, while these responses exert a long-lasting suppressive effect upon network excitability and ongoing activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion summarizing the bidirectional interactions demonstrated in the study.

claim: Visual responses exert a long-lasting suppressive effect upon network excitability and ongoing activity.
source: Ongoing activity shapes the incidental state of neuronal excitability, which in turn modulates visual responses, while these responses exert a long-lasting suppressive effect upon network excitability and ongoing activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion summarizing the bidirectional interactions demonstrated in the study.

claim: The model predicted an adaptation of tectal visual responses to the common stimulus, but not to the deviant stimulus.
source: The model predicted an adaptation of tectal visual responses to the common stimulus, but not to the deviant stimulus (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model simulation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Adaptation reduced the mean response of model cells tuned to the high elevation stimulus to about 70% of their initial amplitude followed by a partial recovery during the 90 s breaks.
source: Adaptation reduced the mean response of model cells tuned to the high elevation stimulus to about 70% of their initial amplitude followed by a partial recovery during the 90 s breaks (Figure 6A, stars).
evidence: This is an observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The response to the low elevation stimulus remained approximately constant in the model.
source: Conversely, the response to the low elevation stimulus remained approximately constant.
evidence: This is an observation from the model simulation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In experimental data, high-frequency stimulus presentation caused a spatially specific response adaptation to the common stimulus.
source: In agreement with the model prediction, high-frequency stimulus presentation caused a spatially specific response adaptation to the common stimulus.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The adaptation pattern in experimental data matches the predicted combined effect of RGC adaptation and intrinsic tectal dynamics.
source: The adaptation pattern matches the predicted combined effect of RGC adaptation and intrinsic tectal dynamics (Figure 6A), rather than either one alone (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental data and model predictions shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The response to the common (high elevation) stimulus was attenuated in most cells.
source: The response to the common (high elevation) stimulus was attenuated in most cells (Figure 6C–D, cyan), and attenuation magnitude was linearly correlated with the amplitude of the baseline response (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: Attenuation magnitude for the common stimulus was linearly correlated with the amplitude of the baseline response.
source: The response to the common (high elevation) stimulus was attenuated in most cells (Figure 6C–D, cyan), and attenuation magnitude was linearly correlated with the amplitude of the baseline response (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Response modulation to the deviant (low elevation) stimulus was less consistent.
source: By contrast, response modulation to the deviant (low elevation) stimulus was less consistent (Figure 6C–D, yellow), although some attenuation was observed in cells that were strongly activated by the common stimulus (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: Some attenuation to the deviant stimulus was observed in cells that were strongly activated by the common stimulus.
source: By contrast, response modulation to the deviant (low elevation) stimulus was less consistent (Figure 6C–D, yellow), although some attenuation was observed in cells that were strongly activated by the common stimulus (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The common stimulus drives a subset of tectal cells to a suppressed state, which modulates their subsequent responses to either stimulus.
source: These results show that the common stimulus drives a subset of tectal cells to a supressed state, which modulates their subsequent responses to either stimulus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the response modulation analysis.

claim: OT displays experience-dependent response modulation as predicted by the network model.
source: To conclude, OT displays experience-dependent response modulation as predicted by our network model.
evidence: This is a conclusion summarizing the agreement between model predictions and experimental observations.

claim: Experience-dependent response modulation allows for integration of past stimuli and suppression of subsequent responses to similar stimuli.
source: This effect allows for integration of past stimuli and suppression of subsequent responses to similar stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the observed adaptation.

claim: Hunting routines of larval zebrafish invariably commence with eye convergence.
source: Because hunting routines of larval zebrafish invariably commence with eye convergence, we used the occurrence of convergent saccades (CS) to identify prey-catching behavioral responses (Figure 7A inset, Bianco et al., 2011; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013; Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous CSs are associated with an increase in tectal activity, particularly in the anterior tectum.
source: By examining activity in 1 s time windows centred on CSs ('CS-associated activity', Figure 7A, orange shaded area), we found that spontaneous CSs are associated with an increase in tectal activity, particularly in the anterior tectum (Figure 7A–B, anterior tectum p=0.002, n=11 fish, Wilcoxon signed rank test, anterior vs posterior activity p=0.02, n=11 fish, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B with statistical testing.

claim: CS-associated activity was lateralized in accordance with the direction of behavior.
source: Moreover, CS-associated activity was lateralized in accordance with the direction of behavior.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: In anterior OT, CS-associated activity was significantly biased towards the hemisphere contralateral to post-saccadic gaze.
source: In anterior (but not posterior) OT, CS-associated activity was significantly biased towards the hemisphere contralateral to post-saccadic gaze (Figure 7C–D, p=0.003 and 0.7 for anterior and posterior OT, n=408 CSs, two-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 7C-D with statistical testing.

claim: These findings are in agreement with previous reports linking anterior OT activity with prey-catching behavior directed to the contralateral side.
source: These findings are in agreement with previous reports linking anterior OT activity with prey-catching behavior directed to the contralateral side (Fajardo et al., 2013; Bianco and Engert, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Linear drive in anterior OT was significantly elevated prior to CSs.
source: This analysis showed that linear drive in anterior OT was significantly elevated prior to CSs (Figure 7E–F, pre-CS vs baseline p=0.004, n=11 fish, one-tailed t-test), and this difference was larger compared to posterior OT (p=0.04, n=11 fish, one-tailed paired t-test).
evidence: This is an observation from model-estimated linear drive shown in Figure 7E-F with statistical testing.

claim: Pre-CS linear drive was positively correlated with CS-associated activity at a single-cell level.
source: At a single-cell level, pre-CS linear drive was positively correlated with CS-associated activity, both for individual CSs (Figure 7H) as well as for data pooled over all spontaneous CSs (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 7H-I.

claim: These results are compatible with ongoing activity in the tectal network modulating the excitability state of OT neurons and contributing to the generation of spontaneous prey-catching behavior.
source: These results are compatible with ongoing activity in the tectal network modulating the excitability state of OT neurons and contributing to the generation of spontaneous prey-catching behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of pre-CS linear drive and CS-associated activity.

claim: The rate of spontaneous CSs in the 2 min that followed any visual stimulus was reduced by approximately one-third compared to rest blocks.
source: When we analysed spontaneous behavior, we found that the rate of spontaneous CSs in the 2 min that followed any visual stimulus was reduced by approximately one-third compared to rest blocks (Figure 7J, n=13 fish, p=0.002, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral data shown in Figure 7J with statistical testing.

claim: This suppression of behavior is concordant with the lasting reduction in excitability state and ongoing tectal activity.
source: This suppression of behavior is concordant with the lasting reduction in excitability state and ongoing tectal activity described above.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking behavioral observations to previous findings.

claim: The probability of visually evoked prey-catching was modulated by stimulus history in a qualitatively similar way to visually evoked tectal activity.
source: Moreover, the probability of visually evoked prey-catching was modulated by stimulus history in a qualitatively similar way to visually evoked tectal activity.
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Response rates declined for common, but not deviant stimuli.
source: Specifically, response rates declined for common, but not deviant stimuli (Figure 7K, compare Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: The state of the tectal network, reflecting the integration of previous sensory inputs as well as ongoing activity, impacts both spontaneous and visually evoked prey-catching behavior.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that the state of the tectal network, reflecting the integration of previous sensory inputs as well as ongoing activity, impacts both spontaneous and visually evoked prey-catching behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral observations.

claim: A recurrent interaction motif incorporating fast, local excitation and long-lasting, activity-dependent suppression was sufficient to reproduce the occurrence and statistics of tectal bursting.
source: Based on observations of ongoing, 'spontaneous', activity, we inferred a recurrent circuit motif incorporating fast, local excitation and long-lasting, activity-dependent suppression, which was sufficient to reproduce the occurrence and statistics of tectal bursting.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the modeling work.

claim: Applying recurrent interactions to recent activity inferred from calcium recordings gave a means to predict the excitability state of tectal neurons and thereby explain a portion of the variability in visually evoked responses.
source: Applying these same recurrent interactions to recent activity inferred from calcium recordings gave us a means to predict the (usually unseen) excitability state of tectal neurons and thereby explain a portion of the variability in visually evoked responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from applying the model to experimental data.

claim: Prolonged recurrent suppression explained the lasting effect of sensory stimuli on ongoing tectal dynamics as well as spatially selective visual response adaptation.
source: Prolonged recurrent suppression explained the lasting effect of sensory stimuli on ongoing tectal dynamics as well as spatially selective visual response adaptation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the adaptation experiments.

claim: Model-predicted network state explained variability in prey-catching responses.
source: Finally, model-predicted network state explained variability in prey-catching responses, suggest these recurrent interactions are relevant to tectally mediated behavior.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the behavioral experiments.

claim: A recurrent interaction motif can account for bidirectional interactions between neuronal activity and network state, which contribute to variability in sensory encoding and behavior.
source: In sum, our findings suggest that a recurrent interaction motif can account for bidirectional interactions between neuronal activity and network state, which contribute to variability in sensory encoding and behavior.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Despite being defined by only seven parameters, the minimal motif supported the emergence of stochastic tectal bursting with biologically realistic statistics.
source: Despite being defined by only seven parameters, this minimal motif supported the emergence of stochastic tectal bursting with biologically realistic statistics.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results.

claim: The model explained some of the variability in visually evoked activity, the effect of that activity on network state, visual response adaptation and spatially specific behavioral habituation.
source: The model also explained some of the variability in visually evoked activity, the effect of that activity on network state, visual response adaptation and spatially specific behavioral habituation, suggesting this recurrent interaction motif is a dominant feature of the optic tectum.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's explanatory power.

claim: Applying the same connectivity rule with identical parameters across every tectal neuron is an oversimplification.
source: However, applying the same connectivity rule, with identical parameters, across every tectal neuron is certainly an oversimplification and our model should not be regarded as a detailed approximation of tectal connectivity.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the model's limitations.

claim: More expressive models that accommodate cell-specific connectivity parameters are expected to provide more accurate quantitative predictions.
source: Indeed, although it qualitatively reproduced several biological observations, model predictions deviated quantitatively and more expressive models that accommodate cell-specific connectivity parameters are expected to provide more accurate quantitative predictions.
evidence: This is a speculation about future model improvements.

claim: Biologically realistic localised bursting can emerge in a network where there are no assemblies and the same connectivity motif is implemented identically for every cell.
source: However, here we show that biologically realistic localised bursting can emerge in a network in which, by design, there are no assemblies; rather the same connectivity motif (in which recurrent interactions smoothly decay with distance) is implemented identically for every cell.
evidence: This is a key finding from the modeling work that challenges previous interpretations.

claim: Localised bursting, by itself, is insufficient evidence for heterogeneities in connectivity such as assemblies.
source: Although, as discussed above, our model is certainly and oversimplification and does not rule out the existence of assemblies, it highlights that localised bursting, by itself, is insufficient evidence for such heterogeneities in connectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the interpretation of bursting activity.

claim: Recurrent connections have been demonstrated by intracellular recording of delayed excitatory post-synaptic potentials in tadpole tectum following optic tract stimulation.
source: Such connections have been demonstrated by intracellular recording of delayed excitatory post-synaptic potentials in tadpole tectum following optic tract stimulation (Pratt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Delayed glutamatergic potentials were recorded in slices from rat superior colliculus and are thought to mediate pre-saccadic bursting.
source: Delayed glutamatergic potentials were similarly recorded in slices from rat superior colliculus and are thought to mediate pre-saccadic bursting (Saito and Isa, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Long-lasting suppression might be mediated by pre-synaptic depression, which can persist for tens of seconds in the avian OT.
source: This interaction might be mediated by pre-synaptic depression, which can persist for tens of seconds in the avian OT (Luksch et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculation about biological mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: Slow suppression might be mediated by activity-dependent changes in intracellular properties such as ionic concentrations or membrane conductances, potentially lasting for several minutes.
source: Alternatively, slow suppression might be mediated by activity-dependent changes in intracellular properties such as ionic concentrations or membrane conductances, potentially lasting for several minutes (Desai et al., 1999; Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Gasselin et al., 2015; Zylbertal et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is a speculation about biological mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Long-term suppression might derive from activity in inhibitory populations external to OT such as GABAergic populations in the vicinity of the isthmic hindbrain.
source: However, brain regions interconnected with OT, such as GABAergic populations in the vicinity of the isthmic hindbrain (Gebhardt et al., 2019; Henriques et al., 2019), might provide long lasting feedback inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculation about biological mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: The state of the tectal network is predictive of prey-catching response probability, in agreement with the role of OT in generating premotor signals for this visuomotor behavior.
source: Our results indicate that the state of the tectal network is predictive of prey-catching response probability, in agreement with the role of OT in generating premotor signals for this visuomotor behavior (Herrero et al., 1998; Gahtan et al., 2005; Bianco and Engert, 2015; Antinucci et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the behavioral results, supported by citations.

claim: The optic tectum is thought to be involved in detection and selection of salient inputs and generation of rapid behavioral responses.
source: The optic tectum (and its mammalian homolog the superior colliculus), is thought to be involved in detection and selection of salient inputs and generation of rapid behavioral responses (Boehnke and Munoz, 2008; Dutta and Gutfreund, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The experience-dependent activity suppression observed is compatible with the role of OT in filtering out expected inputs which are less likely to be associated with immediate danger or prey-catching opportunity.
source: The experience-dependent activity suppression we observe is compatible with this role, as it filters out expected inputs which are less likely to be associated with immediate danger or prey-catching opportunity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the observed suppression.

claim: Zebrafish OT exhibits response adaptation to looming stimuli that is thought to play a role in the habituation of escape behavior.
source: Similarly, zebrafish OT exhibits response adaptation to looming stimuli that is thought to play a role in the habituation of escape behavior (Marquez-Legorreta et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Comparable stimulus-selective adaptation and behavioral habituation has been described for auditory stimuli in barn owl OT.
source: Comparable stimulus-selective adaptation and behavioral habituation has been described for auditory stimuli in barn owl OT (Reches and Gutfreund, 2008; Netser et al., 2011), and for overhead looming stimuli in the mouse superior colliculus (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Comparable stimulus-selective adaptation and behavioral habituation has been described for overhead looming stimuli in the mouse superior colliculus.
source: Comparable stimulus-selective adaptation and behavioral habituation has been described for auditory stimuli in barn owl OT (Reches and Gutfreund, 2008; Netser et al., 2011), and for overhead looming stimuli in the mouse superior colliculus (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Adaptation in the barn owl is selective for multiple auditory stimulus features such as interaural time and level differences, as well as frequency and amplitude.
source: Notably, adaptation in the barn owl is selective for multiple auditory stimulus features such as interaural time and level differences, as well as frequency and amplitude.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation.

claim: In the simple model proposed, the strength of interactions between neurons depends solely on Euclidean distance and therefore the spatial proximity of their receptive fields.
source: In the simple model we propose, the strength of interactions between neurons depends solely on Euclidean distance and therefore the spatial proximity of their receptive fields.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model design.
